extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, polished periodical essays and social criticism in the style of The Spectator: moral reflections, translations, letters, and practical counsel aimed at a cultivated public. Emphasises taste, brevity, and instructive anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ridicule to cure love
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ridicule, perhaps, is a better Expedient against Love than sober Advice, and I am of Opinion, that Hudibras and Don Quixote may be as effectual to cure the Extravagancies of this Passion, as any of the old Philosophers.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: employ comic satire or ridicule (examples: Hudibras, Don Quixote) to correct romantic folly rather than earnest moralising. Context: offered as practical counsel to readers suffering from unrequited love; the author will publish a related (possibly spurious) Greek manuscript as illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling inquisitive persons (do not trust them with secrets)
rubrics_metrics.description: "As the Inquisitive, in my Opinion, are such merely from a Vacancy in their own Imaginations... there is nothing, methinks, so dangerous as to communicate Secrets to them; for the same Temper of Enquiry makes them as impertinently communicative.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational rule for social interaction: inquisitive people serve as funnels/channels of conversation — they collect and pass along scraps of information verbatim; avoid confiding secrets to them; if one wishes to correct or contradict a rumour, supply the inquisitive person yourself (they will repeat it). Examples given of trivial gossip repeated in public rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental control of noisy talkers (the 'Licinius' pipe)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To remedy this Excess, he had an ingenious Servant... always attended him with a Pitch-pipe, or Instrument to regulate the Voice... any of their Hearers have a very good Title to play a soft Note in their own Defence.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical proposal: manufacture and deploy a regulating instrument (modernised 'Licinius') to check loud talkers in public settings; include an improvement called a 'Hush-Note' for long stories, swearing, obscenity, etc. Suggested distribution: lodge at coffee-houses or carried for private use; author will notify likely offenders privately (advice: 'Get a Licinius').

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of an orator: organs of speech and appropriate modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: "the several Organs of Speech which an Orator ought to have in Perfection, as the Tongue, the Teeth [the Lips,] the Nose, the Palate, and the Wind-pipe... you have omitted the most material Organ of them all, and that is the Forehead.", and "Cicero tells us that he never liked an Orator who did not appear in some little Confusion at the Beginning of his Speech... Trembling and Concern... is a sort of Deference... raises a Benevolence in the Audience.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance criteria for public speaking: cultivate clear pronunciation and articulation (attention to tongue, teeth, lips, nose, palate, wind‑pipe — figuratively 'forehead' as presence); modesty/nervousness at the outset is favourable and gains audience sympathy. Avoid excessive bashfulness (which prevents performance) and avoid mere impudence without modesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of youth: curriculum and pedagogy for polite learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "My Design is to retire with them to an agreeable Solitude... instructed in Musick, Dancing, Drawing, Designing... these Accomplishments... might make as proper Diversions... acquaint them with some of the most polite English Writers... Masters of the Latin Tongue by Methods far easier than those in Lilly... exercise their Style in Writing any light Pieces... frequently in their Native Language... run over together with them the best Roman Historians, Poets, and Orators, and point out their more remarkable Beauties.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive programme for educating genteel youth: combine accomplishments (music, dance, drawing) with early exposure to good English writing to cultivate taste; introduce Latin after taste is formed, use easier methods than traditional grammars; use recitation, acting (Terence, Sophocles, Shakespeare), medals, chronology, geography, and light writing exercises in the native tongue to awaken imagination and patriotism. Aim: form taste, moral imagination, and facility in languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation criterion: preserve brevity, turn of expression, and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of three translations of a Sappho fragment: "the three first Stanzas are rendred almost Word for Word, and not only with the same Elegance, but with the same short Turn of Expression... Monsieur Boileau... is rather an Imitation than a Translation... he has given us all the Poetry, but not all the Passion of this famous Fragment.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation standard for translating lyric poetry: prefer translations that maintain the original's concise turns of expression and the immediacy/vehemence of emotion (passion), not merely poetic paraphrase. Use classical criticism (Longinus) as authority for judging fidelity to natural representation of emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as a virtue and its vices
rubrics_metrics.description: "A just and reasonable Modesty does not only recommend Eloquence, but sets off every great Talent... Modesty is not only an Ornament, but also a Guard to Virtue... If Modesty has so great an Influence... what can more undermine Morality than that Politeness... which treats as unfashionable the most ingenuous Part of our Behaviour... recommends Impudence as good Breeding..." and identification of 'vicious Modesty' (ashamed to act upon reason) and 'vicious Modesty' about birth/profession/poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral criterion for personal conduct and character: cultivate modesty to enhance virtue and social reception; beware two corruptions — (1) false modesty that prevents acting on rational duty, and (2) shame about unavoidable circumstances (birth, poverty) which undermines noble conduct. Politeness that rewards shamelessness is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy on alms and beggary (work-before-relief principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We Merchants... ought never to encourage Beggars. ...no Man should be permitted to take Relief from the Parish, or to ask it in the Street, till he has first purchased as much as possible of his own Livelihood by the Labour of his own Hands; and then the Publick ought only to be taxed to make good the Deficiency.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive social-economic standard: charitable relief should be conditional on prior effort or provision of labour; unearned alms are 'the Wages of Idleness' and perpetuate dependence, harm domestic manufacture and consumption, and benefit landed interests and excise. Practical effect envisaged: increase labour supply and reduce prices of manufactures.
